chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah who said:

I asked him about buying the green plants (al-qasheel). The man buys it and does not cut it, and it begins to sprout during his leaving it until its ear emerges as barley or wheat. And he had bought it from its origin upon a stipulation that whatever there is of the tax (kharaj) is upon the non-Muslim (al-'ilj). So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If he stipulated when he bought it that if he so desires he would cut it, and if he so desires he would leave it as it is until it becomes an ear, otherwise it is not befitting for him that he leaves it until it becomes an ear.'

key_terms.الْعِلْجِ: The non-Muslim (specifically referring to the dhimmi or landowner in this context)
key_terms.الْقَصِيلِ: Green plants or crops before they are fully dried and harvested
key_terms.خَرَاجٍ: Land tax or tribute, often paid by non-Muslims in early Islamic context
key_terms.سُنْبُلُهُ: Its ear (referring to the grain head of barley or wheat)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on buying and selling green plants before harvest, and how does the stipulation of options affect the transaction?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of selling unharvested crops (qasheel) by establishing that the buyer's right to cut early depends on explicit stipulation at the time of sale; without such a condition, leaving the crop to mature is the default. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on contractual precision (shart) in agricultural transactions to prevent ambiguity (gharar) and ensure fair usage of land resources. The ruling reflects the practical concerns of early Islamic agrarian society regarding tax obligations (kharaj) and the economic value of straw versus grain.
